clue.text: Signs up mountain eccentric figures should support

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting part sits underneath, so it comes second in the entry
in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain
a card is an eccentric or amusing character

explanation.surface: Odd-looking figures are propping up signposts on a mountain path.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the supporting piece sits underneath. 'Figures' suggests numbers, but here they are people: a card is a comic character.
explanation.definitionFit: Placards are boards carrying printed notices, held up at protests or posted on walls.

clue.text: Week everyone put to work for beer and punch

definitions.note: the answer means both beer and a punch

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for week
everyone is all of them
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Everyone is made to work for a week and is paid in beer and punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to' simply places OP after the rest. 'Punch' looks like a party drink beside beer, but it is a blow; wallop is British slang for both a heavy blow and beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallop is informal British for a hard hit and also an old slang word for ale or bitter.

clue.text: Figure crossing river suffered surge in west

indicators.note: whatever crosses over another thing straddles it, lying on both sides

parts.note: seven is a number, a figure
R is the usual abbreviation for river
to bear is to suffer, past tense bore

explanation.surface: Someone crossing a river in the west of England was hit by a surge of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' suggests a person crossing the river, but it is a number. The Severn is Britain's longest river, flowing past Gloucester into the Bristol Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A bore is a tidal wave running upriver, and the one on England's western Severn estuary is famous among surfers.

clue.text: Slight exasperation shown about good number

indicators.note: about means around, so one part is wrapped round the rest

parts.note: ire is anger or annoyance
G is the standard abbreviation for good
No. is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: Mild irritation is shown about a pleasing figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as an adjective meaning small, but it is a verb: to slight someone is to snub them.
explanation.definitionFit: To slight a person is to snub them or treat them as unworthy of notice, which is a deliberate brush-off.

clue.text: Luxuriant hairstyle publicity worker covers

indicators.note: whatever covers something is wrapped over and round it

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement
a bun is hair coiled at the back of the head
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: A thick, glossy hairstyle is hidden beneath a publicist's covers.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces after the hairstyle together wrap round it. 'Luxuriant' sits beside 'hairstyle' as if describing it, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Luxuriant growth is rich and profuse, and plentiful in amount is what the answer means too.

clue.text: Printed material endlessly creates confusion

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a blurb is the promotional text printed on a book jacket

explanation.surface: Paperwork that never ends causes muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: BLURB loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A blur is something indistinct or a hazy muddle, as when events pass in a whirl you cannot recall.

clue.text: Height conserved by two insects and huge beast

indicators.note: what is conserved is kept safely held inside something else

parts.note: a bee and a moth
H is the abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: Two small insects and an enormous animal are oddly sharing one sentence about conservation.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes inside BEE, then MOTH follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Behemoth is a colossal creature in the Book of Job, now used for anything enormous and monstrous.

clue.text: Getting close to pheasant in hunting land is simple

indicators.note: placed in means set inside something else

parts.note: a chase is an unenclosed area of land kept for hunting

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the bird

explanation.surface: Getting near a pheasant on a shooting estate is easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting close to' reads like approaching the bird, but it only picks its last letter. A chase, as in Cannock Chase, is old English hunting ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste style is plain and unadorned, so it is restrained and free of ornament or fuss.

clue.text: Great time involves rugby starting later back where play occurs

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read from right to left
to involve is to take in, so one part goes inside another

parts.note: to have a ball is to have a great time

indicators.note: if the start comes later than the word does, its first letter is missing

parts.note: rugger is the informal British name for rugby union

explanation.surface: A great time watching rugby starts late, at the back of the ground where play goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: BALL holds UGGER to make the British slang 'bugger all' (nothing at all), which reversed is Dylan Thomas's joke name. 'Play' sounds like sport, but it is a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Llareggub is the fictional Welsh seaside town in which Dylan Thomas set his radio drama Under Milk Wood.

clue.text: Scrounger having caught fish returned horse

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
an eel is a long fish

explanation.surface: A freeloader who caught a fish sends back a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: H, C and EEL are strung together and then the whole string is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A leech is a person who clings to others and sponges off them, like the bloodsucking worm.

clue.text: Drop a little lower keeping length in mind

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one part is held inside

parts.note: cave is Latin for beware, used in English schools as a warning: mind out
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: Lower something gently while keeping the length in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as move down, but it is one that lows, a cow; its little one is a calf, and to drop a calf is to give birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers say a cow drops her young, and the verb for a cow giving birth is exactly this word.

clue.text: Stray slow seen heading for recreation ground

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed and broken up, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its top, so just its opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dawdling stray dog is spotted making for the park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recreation ground' looks like one phrase, a park, but it splits into a letter source and the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stray animal has no keeper or home, so it belongs to nobody at all.

clue.text: Perhaps reprimand from Caedmon for USWNT star?

parts.note: a rap is a rebuke, as in a rap over the knuckles
Caedmon was the earliest named English poet, who wrote in Old English, OE

explanation.surface: Would a seventh-century poet scold an American footballer?
explanation.walkthrough: A rebuke coming from Caedmon would be a RAP IN OE, Old English. USWNT is the United States Women's National Team in soccer.
explanation.definitionFit: Megan Rapinoe is a World Cup-winning forward and long-time captain of the American women's national football team.

clue.text: American doctor sprang up to give name

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree
to spring up is to rise, past tense rose

explanation.surface: An American doctor leapt up to announce a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' has many crossword abbreviations (DR, MO, GP, MD); this one is MB.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrose is a man's first name, borne by the fourth-century bishop of Milan who became a saint.

clue.text: Having less hair — bit rubbish?

parts.note: more bald means having less hair
a dash is a small amount, a bit

explanation.surface: Is going a little thinner on top a bit of a disaster?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' looks like a verdict on the hair loss, but it is the definition, meaning nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Balderdash is senseless talk or writing, nonsense, which is what rubbish means in speech.

clue.text: Bloomer from principal in West Bank city?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read cryptically: the leading performer of a Palestinian town

explanation.surface: A head teacher in a Palestinian city has made an embarrassing mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' is British slang for a blunder, but here it is a thing that blooms. Read literally, the star of Bethlehem is the town's principal.
explanation.definitionFit: Star-of-Bethlehem is a bulb plant with starry white flowers, while the nativity star guided the Magi to Bethlehem.

clue.text: African mammal drivers run over crossing road

indicators.note: to cross something is to span it, so these letters lie on either side

parts.note: the AA, the Automobile Association, is a British motoring organisation for drivers
RD is the abbreviation for road

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means flipped so it reads upwards

parts.note: water runs or flows

explanation.surface: A motorist runs over an African animal as it crosses the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' looks like a road accident, but splits into a word and its reversal signal. The AA is Britain's Automobile Association, a breakdown service for motorists.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardwolf is a small striped hyena of southern and eastern Africa that feeds mainly on termites.

clue.text: £50 in pocket? Have fine attire

indicators.note: whatever is put in something ends up held inside it

parts.note: to pocket something is to bag it
L is the pound sign's letter (libra) and L is the Roman numeral for 50
to have is to own

explanation.surface: With fifty pounds in your pocket, you can afford smart clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: '£50' splits into L for pound and L for fifty, which go inside BAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballgown is a long formal dress worn to a dance, the finest kind of evening wear.

clue.text: Commute time halved after motorway opening

indicators.note: cut in half, so only the first two of the four letters survive
one piece placed after another simply follows it in the answer

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI
taken as written
a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: A journey to work takes half as long once the motorway opens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commute' suggests a drive to the office, but it is a verb as in commuting a sentence. M1 becomes MI by reading the digit as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To commute a punishment is to reduce its severity, which is to lessen or soften it.

clue.text: Strange for all to see bishop stopping confirmation

indicators.note: something that stops a gap plugs it, so it goes inside

parts.note: a seal confirms or ratifies an agreement
U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for everyone
RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title

explanation.surface: It is odd that, in public view, a bishop halts a confirmation service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confirmation' looks like the church rite, which suits the bishop, but it is a seal of approval. U is the British film rating for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Surreal describes something bizarre and dreamlike, like a Dali painting, so it is weird or odd.

clue.text: Buy saw forged underground across the pond

indicators.note: forged metal is beaten into a new shape, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone buys a counterfeit tool in a criminal underworld in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across the pond' means in America; in Britain the same word is a pedestrian tunnel under a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call an urban metro railway running in tunnels by this name, where Londoners say the Tube.

clue.text: Stop media manipulation happening

parts.note: PR is public relations, managing how the press presents things
an event is something that happens

explanation.surface: A call to halt the spin doctoring going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' reads as an imperative addressed to the media, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevent something is to keep it from occurring, which is to halt or block it.

clue.text: Stickler in bad mood about Bible book

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one part wraps round another

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking, as in being in a pet
Dan. is the abbreviation for the Book of Daniel

explanation.surface: A fussy person is in a foul temper about a Bible passage.
explanation.walkthrough: A pet in this sense is a sulk; being 'in a pet' is mainly British. Bible books are routinely shortened in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on exact rules and small details, as does someone overly fussy about accuracy.

clue.text: Wembley content with minute sign

indicators.note: the content of something is what lies inside it, so the outer edges are dropped

parts.note: the name of the stadium
M is the abbreviation for minute

explanation.surface: A crowd at Wembley is pleased with a gesture made in the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like an adjective meaning happy, but it is a noun: the contents. Wembley is England's national football stadium in London.
explanation.definitionFit: An emblem is a symbolic badge or device, such as a national flower, representing something larger.

clue.text: Asked to adopt bird with deformed limbs?

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one part is taken inside

parts.note: to beg is to ask earnestly
an owl is a bird

explanation.surface: A request to take in a lame bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird goes in after the first letter, splitting the verb. 'Deformed' sounds like an anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow legs curve outward at the knee, a bend in the legs that leaves a gap between them.

clue.text: Language very lacking in poetry

indicators.note: what lacks something is missing it, so letters are taken out

parts.note: verse is poetry
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A tongue with no real poetry in it.
explanation.walkthrough: VERSE lacks V. 'Very lacking' reads as 'badly lacking', but 'very' supplies the letter removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, a Celtic tongue common in crosswords.

clue.text: Girl with user guide starts to remove disc errors

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, a young society woman

indicators.note: the start of each word is its opening letter, so only those are kept

parts.note: first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A girl reads the manual to start fixing faults on her disk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' could seem to begin the definition, but it picks the first letters of the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Programmers clear faults from software or storage by finding and fixing them, the process named here.

clue.text: Worldly hold-up man eventually scratching back

indicators.note: to scratch is to strike out, and the back is the rear, so the last letter goes

parts.note: at last means eventually

explanation.surface: A worldly-wise robber ends up scratching his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold-up man' looks like a robber, but it is the Titan who held up the heavens, which later art shows as the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan Atlas was condemned to bear the sky on his shoulders, often pictured carrying the Earth.

clue.text: Expressed deep unhappiness with snakes affected by gale

parts.note: a road that snakes winds back and forth
crying shows deep sadness

explanation.surface: Someone cried bitterly over snakes caught in a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snakes' looks like a noun, the reptiles, but it is a verb meaning twists. 'With' lets the two pieces come in either order.
explanation.definitionFit: A windswept place or person is exposed to strong blasts of air and shows it, buffeted and dishevelled.
